cards.title: Marketing as creating conditions for an idea to spread
cards.summary: Define marketing as creating the conditions for an idea to spread rather than interrupting people to push average products, and rewire your store's operating priorities accordingly.
cards.use_when: Setting the strategic direction for a store or brand — deciding where to invest effort between paid interruption, product quality and referral conditions.

cards.title: The remarkable benchmark: worth making a remark about
cards.summary: Test whether a product is genuinely remarkable — literally worth a customer making a remark about — before assuming word-of-mouth will carry it.
cards.use_when: Product selection or product development decisions: evaluating whether a new SKU or hero product can generate organic word-of-mouth.

cards.title: Don't play the algorithm game if your audience isn't there
cards.summary: Build an audience through other people talking about you rather than chasing algorithmic reach, especially when the platform persona doesn't fit you.
cards.use_when: Deciding which acquisition and content channels to invest in — particularly when the founder or brand is expected to perform on social platforms that don't suit them.

cards.title: Vanity reach is a false proxy — measure sales, not views
cards.summary: Treat large view counts that produce trivial revenue as a trap; judge organic efforts by what they actually sell.
cards.use_when: Evaluating organic content performance, influencer campaigns or viral video results for a store.

cards.title: Copy proven business models; originality is overrated
cards.summary: Use an existing business structure rather than inventing a new one — innovate on the product story and experience, not the operating model.
cards.use_when: Planning a new store, launching a new brand line, or choosing an operating model (dropship, private label, wholesale, subscription).

cards.title: Sell the story, not the object: status, affiliation, tension
cards.summary: Once basic needs are met, purchases are stories about status and affiliation; build enough tension that not buying becomes uncomfortable.
cards.use_when: Writing product pages, brand messaging or launch copy — deciding what the product page is actually selling.

cards.title: Tension and story structure for a launch dinner test
cards.summary: Most people already tell great stories socially; apply the same structure to your offer — who it's for, what's at stake, what possibility it opens.
cards.use_when: Drafting launch messaging, email invitations, event or drop announcements where you need people to say yes.

cards.title: Radical empathy: sell what you wouldn't buy yourself
cards.summary: Overcome the impostor feeling of selling something you personally wouldn't buy by doing practical empathy for the customer who genuinely needs it.
cards.use_when: When founder discomfort or impostor syndrome is blocking product selection, marketing copy or outbound effort.

cards.title: Design for the smallest viable market, not everyone
cards.summary: Pick the smallest group you can profitably serve and build specifically for them; a narrow niche with four proven clients beats a generic offer to all comers.
cards.use_when: Product selection, brand positioning or service definition — deciding who the store is for and, explicitly, who it is not for.

cards.title: Good decisions can fail; separate decision quality from outcome
cards.summary: Judge business decisions on the process and the odds, not on whether they happened to work out, so you can commit to a focused bet without false confidence.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to commit to a niche, a product line, a channel or a price change — and when evaluating past experiments at a retro.

cards.title: Practical empathy experimentation: find who lights up
cards.summary: Run small, real-world tests with a handful of people and watch who responds — that trains your offer and you iterate from there.
cards.use_when: Early product validation and creative testing: choosing a niche, an offer, a headline or an ad angle before scaling spend.

cards.title: Match the story to existing worldviews and context
cards.summary: Start from what your audience already believes and the context they are in; changing a worldview is far harder than affirming one.
cards.use_when: Choosing target segments, ad creative angles and channel context — especially when a campaign underperforms despite good execution.

cards.title: Consistency is a brand promise; authenticity is for amateurs
cards.summary: Deliver the promised version of your brand on every touchpoint regardless of how you feel, because customers bought the promise, not your mood.
cards.use_when: Customer service standards, shipping and fulfillment consistency, and repeat-touchpoint design such as subscriptions, email and support responses.

cards.title: Make the customer the word-spreader: design for conversation
cards.summary: Build the conditions for customers to spread the word by giving them something they gain from telling — not by spamming or begging for shares.
cards.use_when: Referral program design, unboxing and packaging decisions, community building and post-purchase email sequences.

cards.title: Show up persistently: earn permission, then enrollment
cards.summary: Publish and serve reliably for years to earn permission to follow up and to teach — underrated in a fast-moving market.
cards.use_when: Long-term content and email strategy: building an owned audience list for a store and deciding whether to keep going after early quiet.

cards.title: The Dip: locate it before you start, and quit early, not mid-way
cards.summary: Identify the hardest point of a venture before starting; if you lack resources or stamina to survive it, don't start — and most people quit too late, not too soon.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or continue a demanding store initiative — a new category, a long content commitment, a costly product line — or deciding to shut one down.

cards.title: The Dip framework applied to store projects
cards.summary: Use the before-you-start dip check and the 'quit early not mid-dip' rule to choose which store initiatives to launch, pause or kill.
cards.use_when: Portfolio or roadmap decisions: whether to launch a new hero product, commit to a category, or stop an underperforming initiative.

cards.title: Positioning Is About the Prospect's Mind, Not Your Product
cards.summary: Positioning means manipulating what already exists in the customer's mind—the product ladder—rather than inventing something new.
cards.use_when: Choosing a market position, category entry angle, or brand claim for a store or product line before writing any PDP or ad copy.

cards.title: The 'Against' Position: How to Be No. 2
cards.summary: If you are not the leader, position against the leader rather than pretending to be one, as Avis did against Hertz.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative, brand taglines or comparison landing pages for a store or product that is not the market leader.

cards.title: The Uncola Move: Positioning by What You Are Not
cards.summary: Define your brand by the category norm you reject, the way 7-Up positioned as the 'Uncola' rather than as a cola variant.
cards.use_when: Differentiating a product in a crowded category where every competitor claims the same attributes—beverages, supplements, apparel, software.

cards.title: Repositioning the Competition: Undermining the Leader's Concept
cards.summary: Attack the concept the leader owns, not the leader's product, the way Tylenol repositioned aspirin by questioning the stomach-bleeding side effect.
cards.use_when: Planning comparative ad campaigns, review-content angles or landing pages where you need to shift the prospect's view of the incumbent rather than out-shout it.

cards.title: Factory Creneau vs. Mind Creneau
cards.summary: A gap in your product line is not the same as a gap in the customer's perception; only the latter is a real positioning opportunity.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new SKU, sub-brand or category entry, especially when the gap is obvious on a spreadsheet.

cards.title: The Initials Trap: When Abbreviations Dilute Your Brand
cards.summary: Initials and acronyms as brand names only work after a brand is already famous; using them earlier throws away the memory value of a real name.
cards.use_when: Naming or renaming a store, private-label line or sub-brand and choosing between a descriptive/coined name and a set of initials.

cards.title: Coined Names: The One Condition for Using Them
cards.summary: A coined name is acceptable only when you are first in the mind with an absolutely new product.
cards.use_when: Choosing a brand name for a genuinely new product category, new store concept or novel private label, rather than a new SKU in an existing category.

cards.title: The 5 Rules of the Road for House Name vs. New Name
cards.summary: Use five criteria—volume, competition, ad support, significance and distribution—to decide whether a new product rides the house name or gets its own.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand architecture for a line extension: whether a new SKU, category or sub-brand should carry the house brand or a separate name.

cards.title: The Line-Extension Trap and Why It Dilutes the Brand
cards.summary: Extending a strong name across distinctly different products erodes the meaning of that name in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Planning catalog expansion, adding a new category under an existing store brand, or evaluating a tempting free-ride addition.

cards.title: The Teeter-Totter Principle of Category Ownership
cards.summary: One brand name cannot stand for two distinctly different products without one side going down.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a store brand should own multiple categories, or during a product roadmap review before approving a stretch SKU.

cards.title: The Shopping-List Test for a Diffuse Brand
cards.summary: If customers cannot use your brand name as a generic substitute on a shopping list, the name has become too diffuse to position.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a store brand is losing meaning, or screening a proposed extension before it further dilutes the name.

cards.title: The Bartender Test and the Limits of Brand Recall
cards.summary: Use a simple recall test to check whether a brand name evokes its category before you commit marketing spend to it.
cards.use_when: Validating a new store or product name, or measuring whether current branding has actually lodged a category association.

cards.title: Positioning Is What You Do to the Prospect's Mind, Not the Product
cards.summary: Define positioning as securing a slot in the prospect's mind, then use that slot to guide every product, price, place, and promotion decision in your store.
cards.use_when: You're setting or auditing your store's overall brand direction before a range review, rebrand, or category expansion.

cards.title: Prioritize Being First Over Being Best in a New Product Category
cards.summary: If you can be the first credible entrant in a category or use case, that mental slot beats having a superior product — look for what you can be first in before competing head-on.
cards.use_when: You're choosing which new product, category, or niche to launch or how to frame your store's claim.

cards.title: Map Your Category's Product Ladder Before Setting Strategy
cards.summary: Draw the mental ladder of brands shoppers actually rank in your category so your positioning plan starts from the competitor's rung, not a vacuum.
cards.use_when: You're writing a positioning brief, planning a relaunch, or deciding how to differentiate on PDP copy and acquisition creative.

cards.title: Build an 'Against' Position When You Can't Take the Leader Head-On
cards.summary: Position your brand explicitly relative to the category leader — acknowledging their strength — so you create a clear alternative slot instead of an anonymous claim.
cards.use_when: You're a number-two or later entrant in an established category and need a differentiation strategy for your homepage, PDP, and ad creative.

cards.title: Use the 'Not' Frame to Introduce a New Product Category
cards.summary: When launching a genuinely new product or category, explain it against what the prospect already knows, because the mind has no room for something with no relation to the old.
cards.use_when: You're launching a novel product, format, or bundle and need PDP and landing-page framing that makes it instantly understandable.

cards.title: Oversimplify the Message to Cut Into an Overcommunicated Mind
cards.summary: Treat your communication as a selection project: sharpen one message until it can penetrate a saturated mind rather than trying to transmit everything about the product.
cards.use_when: You're deciding what goes on a homepage hero, PDP first screen, or acquisition ad when you have many possible claims.

cards.title: Design for the Prospect's Expectations, Because They Filter Reality
cards.summary: Expectation shapes experience — set high, accurate expectations and avoid priming a negative belief that shoppers will then confirm.
cards.use_when: You're writing PDP copy, product names, or ad creative for a product whose quality or taste/effect is judged subjectively.

cards.title: Reposition by Offering a Fresh Perspective, Not a Better Product
cards.summary: The classic repositioning play is a perspective gap — the product was always capable of what you now claim; you simply make the claim first.
cards.use_when: You sell a commodity or undifferentiated product and need a claim that changes how shoppers categorize you without changing the product.

cards.title: Admit Your Rank Instead of Pretending to Be the Leader
cards.summary: For a non-leader, acknowledging rank honestly is a credible basis for a differentiated position rather than a false claim of superiority.
cards.use_when: You're an unranked or number-two store in a category and need honest, differentiated messaging that feels credible to shoppers.

cards.title: Run the Shopping-List Test to Check for Brand Dilution
cards.summary: If shoppers use your brand name as shorthand for a whole category rather than one specific product, your name has become too generic to carry a specific position.
cards.use_when: You're evaluating whether a brand name has become diluted before extending it to a new product line or category.

cards.title: Apply the Five 'Rules of the Road' When Deciding Between a House Name and a New Name
cards.summary: Use five criteria — expected volume, competition, advertising support, significance, and distribution — to choose whether an extension should borrow the house name or launch under a new one.
cards.use_when: You're planning a product line extension or new category entry and must decide whether to reuse your existing brand name or create a new one.

cards.title: Connect Every Extension Back to the Parent Brand's Meaning
cards.summary: Successful line extensions stay tied to the parent brand's defined meaning, customers, and channel; disconnection dilutes the parent and the extension alike.
cards.use_when: You're adding a SKU, flavor, size, or adjacent category to an existing brand and want the extension to strengthen rather than dilute the parent.

cards.title: Let the Free-Ride Trap Guide How Far You Stretch a Brand
cards.summary: Assume that you cannot ride a second product on the coattails of a famous name — expand a brand only as far as its specific association actually travels.
cards.use_when: You're deciding whether to put an existing store or brand name on an adjacent product range, and want to anticipate where the name stops helping.

cards.title: Use the Teeter-Totter Principle When One Name Risks Standing for Two Products
cards.summary: When one name is used for two distinctly different products, the source's teeter-totter principle says one side goes down — anticipate which one and plan the trade-off.
cards.use_when: You're considering putting an existing brand name on a second, genuinely different product and need to assess the risk to both.

cards.title: Use Six Questions to Start a Positioning Program
cards.summary: Begin with the scout's questions rather than the communicator's — understand the prospect's mental terrain before deciding what to say about your store.
cards.use_when: You're kicking off a positioning or rebrand effort and need a starting checklist before spending on channels.

cards.title: Become an Outside-In Thinker to Hold a Position Over Time
cards.summary: The book's behavioral requirement for successful positioning is thinking from the prospect's perspective with patience, courage, and strength of character rather than from the product outward.
cards.use_when: You're setting up an ongoing positioning program and need the operating mindset that keeps it consistent across launches and campaigns.

cards.title: Find a Window in the Market and Concentrate on a Narrow Target
cards.summary: Because the market is saturated with messages, success comes from selecting narrow targets and timing claims to a receptive window rather than broadcasting broadly.
cards.use_when: You're planning launch timing and audience selection for a new product or campaign.

cards.title: Distinguish the Product Era, Image Era, and Positioning Era When Choosing Messaging
cards.summary: Recognize the shift from product features to brand image to positioning, and build your current strategy on positioning because me-too products and me-too image campaigns undermined the first two approaches.
cards.use_when: You're reviewing your acquisition creative and deciding whether to lead with features, brand imagery, or a positioning claim.

cards.title: Occupy the No. 2 position against the leader
cards.summary: If you can't be first in a category, build your brand position by explicitly relating yourself to the leader rather than attacking head-on.
cards.use_when: Choosing positioning for a store or brand entering a category where a dominant competitor already owns the top rung in customer minds (e.g., a new gear shop vs. an established giant).

cards.title: Find an open 'creneau' inside the prospect's mind, not the factory
cards.summary: Look for an unoccupied position in the customer's mind and claim it first, rather than filling a product gap that only makes sense internally.
cards.use_when: Deciding what new product, size, or category to launch or how to angle a product-page headline for a crowded category.

cards.title: Use price as a positioning claim, stated in advance
cards.summary: High price and low price are each valid positions if you're first to claim them with a credible product story, and the position should be set in your messaging before the customer reaches the store.
cards.use_when: Setting price tier strategy or writing pricing-related copy for a product line or category page.

cards.title: Reposition the competitor to create space in the customer's mind
cards.summary: When no open position exists, move an existing competitor out of the mental slot by making the customer change their view of that competitor's product.
cards.use_when: Entering a saturated category where all obvious positions are taken and you need a wedge for your brand story or comparison content.

cards.title: Leader strategy: reinforce the first position instead of repeating 'we're No. 1'
cards.summary: If you own the top position, advertise the product category's value and your original claim rather than boasting about rank.
cards.use_when: Writing brand messaging or category pages when your store genuinely owns the leading mental position in a niche.

cards.title: Cover competitive moves with a separate brand, not a stretched one
cards.summary: Protect a leading position by launching a distinctly named product for new concepts instead of extending the existing brand into a new meaning.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new sub-brand, product line, or SKU versus attaching a new variant to your best-selling brand.

cards.title: Don't fall into the F.W.M.T.S. trap
cards.summary: After a successful positioning campaign, keep the same position for years instead of drifting into aspiration or new campaigns that abandon what worked.
cards.use_when: Reviewing brand messaging, campaign themes, or homepage copy that has accumulated multiple taglines over time.

cards.title: Check whether you can even 'get there from here'
cards.summary: Before pouring budget into a category push, honestly assess whether your current position makes the goal achievable at all, since effort cannot overcome a structurally hopeless position.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to enter a new product category, compete with a dominant platform, or fund an aggressive growth goal.

cards.title: Avoid the everybody trap and commit to a specific niche
cards.summary: In a crowded market, appeal to everyone dilutes your position; carve out a specific slot even if you lose some customers doing so.
cards.use_when: Writing category, homepage, or brand copy and choosing whether to keep broad, inclusive messaging or commit to a defined customer segment.

cards.title: Make the product name do positioning work
cards.summary: The name is the hook that hangs a brand on the ladder in the customer's mind, and the source calls it the single most important marketing decision.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, private label, or sub-brand, or diagnosing why a well-positioned offer underperforms.

cards.title: Race on launch speed and budget, not late 'better'
cards.summary: Most me-too products fail because they spend time improving the product while a competitor establishes leadership first; speed, launch budget, and a good name beat incremental superiority.
cards.use_when: Planning a product or category launch, deciding launch timing, naming, and marketing spend against an incumbent.

cards.title: Turn sensory expectation into a merchandising and copy lever
cards.summary: Customers taste and judge what they expect to taste, so ingredient and description language on the page shapes perceived product quality.
cards.use_when: Writing product page copy, ingredient lists, or label descriptions for food, supplements, or any product judged by sensory quality.

cards.title: Competitive ads vs. repositioning ads: know the difference
cards.summary: Most comparative advertising fails because it benchmarks against the leader instead of changing the customer's view of that leader's product.
cards.use_when: Planning comparison content, 'us vs. them' pages, or competitor-focused acquisition creative.

cards.title: Treat equality between top brands as unstable
cards.summary: When two brands run neck and neck, the category is unstable and one will usually pull ahead; that's when extra effort pays off most.
cards.use_when: Timing a promotional push or brand investment in a category where you're roughly tied with a rival for the top spot.

cards.title: Position by a category dimension before rivals do
cards.summary: Sex, age, time of day, distribution channel, and usage intensity are all positionable dimensions — first to claim them wins, latecomers fail.
cards.use_when: Choosing an angle for a new product, line, or landing-page narrative in a mature category where broad claims are taken.

cards.title: Name as the Core Positioning Decision
cards.summary: The product or brand name is the single most important marketing decision because it is the hook that hangs the brand on a ladder in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, brand, SKU or storefront, or deciding whether to rename an existing product line.

cards.title: Descriptive Names Beat Coined Names — Unless You're First
cards.summary: Pick a name that nearly describes the benefit rather than a meaningless coined word, because only a genuine first mover can afford an empty name.
cards.use_when: Deciding between a descriptive name (e.g. Soy Butter, Spray 'n Wash) and a coined or abstract brand name for a new product or store line.

cards.title: Don't Let a Name Become Generic
cards.summary: A name should point to your benefit without sliding all the way into a generic category word, or you lose exclusive rights to it.
cards.use_when: Naming or trademarking a launch SKU, deciding whether to coin a new word for a new product format, or reviewing a product name that has become a category catch-all.

cards.title: Audit Existing Names for Obsolescence and Confusion
cards.summary: Names decay as products and markets change; audit the ladder to spot names that mislead or overlap with competitors.
cards.use_when: Portfolio review: assessing whether a legacy brand or product name still communicates the current offer, or whether a rename is warranted.

cards.title: Test Names and Headlines for Sound, Not Just Look
cards.summary: The mind processes words aurally, so evaluate names, slogans and headlines by how they sound, especially for future voice and podcast channels.
cards.use_when: Choosing a store or product name, writing ad headlines or slogans, or preparing a brand name for voice search and audio advertising.

cards.title: Initials and Acronyms Are a Shortcut Trap
cards.summary: Companies copy IBM's initials and mistake cause for effect — initials work only after a name is already famous.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to brand a new store line, private label or acquisition sub-brand with initials or an acronym, or reviewing a corporate rebrand.

cards.title: Line Extension Blurs a Hard-Won Position
cards.summary: Hanging a known name on a new category fails because the brand name is a surrogate for the original product in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product or category under the existing hero brand name versus creating a new brand or sub-brand, e.g. an existing supplement brand moving into skincare.

cards.title: Use a Distinctly Named Hero SKU to Hold a Feature
cards.summary: Give a product a name that carries the benefit, so the customer has a hook to hang attributes on.
cards.use_when: Naming a flagship SKU or private-label item where you want one benefit to be remembered, e.g. an extended-life battery, a durability claim, or a specific food benefit.

cards.title: New Product, New Ladder, New Name
cards.summary: A truly new product cannot live on a famous name because the famous name occupies a sharply defined rung of a different ladder.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product line in a new category under a company that already owns a position in another category.

cards.title: Use Negative Names to Polarize Instead of Hide
cards.summary: When a product's origin is hidden, prospects suspect a problem; a proudly descriptive name builds 'pride of origin' and a long-term positioning campaign.
cards.use_when: Naming or renaming a product whose origin or formulation is unfamiliar to buyers — alternative ingredients, plant-based or lab-made goods, or a product seen as an imitation.

cards.title: Protect a Position You Already Own
cards.summary: A brand that owns a category position (Kleenex, Hertz, Cadillac, Xerox) holds enormous long-term value; do not spend it on a different category.
cards.use_when: Portfolio and pricing decisions when a hero brand or hero SKU is being considered as a vehicle for a new offer, bundle or adjacent category.

cards.title: Spend Publicity Like a Budget, Not a Habit
cards.summary: Anonymity is an easily squandered resource; a lesser-known product gains far more from publicity than a famous one does.
cards.use_when: Planning a PR push, press outreach or influencer campaign for a new store, brand or hero product, and deciding when to use your best story.

cards.title: Use House Names and Separate Names According to Provenance
cards.summary: How a product was created (internal development vs. acquisition) historically drives naming strategy, but the prospect's mind should be the deciding factor.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether an acquired brand or a newly developed product should carry the parent store/brand name, after an acquisition or a category expansion.

cards.title: Position Against the Future, Not the Past, When Renaming
cards.summary: When a name is obsolete, a foot-in-the-past abbreviation freezes it; a clean new name can reposition the whole company.
cards.use_when: Renaming a store, a legacy product line, or a brand after a pivot, product obsolescence or a merger.

cards.title: Use the Shopping List Test to Diagnose Brand Dilution
cards.summary: A quick test for whether your brand name means one thing or many, by asking what a spouse would bring back from a written shopping list.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product category, sub-brand, or SKU under your existing store/brand name, or evaluating whether an existing catalog is already diluted.

cards.title: Line Extension's Short-Term Sales Illusion
cards.summary: New line extensions create an instant recognition flash and pipeline sales that look strong for months, then fade when reorders do not come.
cards.use_when: Interpreting early sales data after launching a new SKU under an existing brand name, or setting expectations with a founder before a sub-brand launch.

cards.title: Bayer and Protein 21: How Sub-Brands Undercut the Parent
cards.summary: Every extension hung on a strong brand erodes the parent's meaning, shown in falling share for Bayer analgesics and Protein 21 shampoo.
cards.use_when: Considering whether to attach your main brand name to an adjacent product line, ingredient variant, or differently-positioned version.

cards.title: Broadening the Base: Reverse Line Extension
cards.summary: Same product, same package, same name — only the use occasion changes, which is how Johnson's baby shampoo became an adult brand.
cards.use_when: Looking for growth from an existing hero product without launching a new SKU, or planning messaging and landing-page angles for a narrowly perceived product.
